grammar_points.name: 〜て form (te-form connection)

explanation.en:
How it works: The て-form (te-form) is one of the most essential Japanese conjugations. It connects actions in sequence, shows means/method, and links to auxiliary verbs. For godan verbs, the ending changes based on the final consonant.

Example from this song: 目指して (mezashite) = 'aiming for (and...)' — from 目指す (mezasu, 'to aim for') → 目指して (mezashite, te-form)

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べて (tabete)
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行って (itte)
• 読む (yomu, 'to read') → 読んで (yonde)

Note: Te-form rules for godan verbs: す→して, く→いて, ぐ→いで, む/ぶ/ぬ→んで, つ/る/う→って. Exception: 行く → 行って (not 行いて). For ichidan verbs, just replace る with て. Mastering the te-form unlocks many grammar patterns.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 目指す (mezasu, 'to aim for') → 目指して (mezashite, te-form, 'aiming for')

grammar_points.name: 〜ず (classical negative)

explanation.en:
How it works: Replace the negative ない (nai) with ず (zu). This is the classical/literary negative conjunctive form, meaning 'without doing'. It's equivalent to modern ないで (naide).

Example from this song: 構わず (kamawazu) = 'without caring' — from 構う (kamau, 'to care/mind') → 構わない (kamawanai, negative) → 構わず (kamawazu)

More examples:
• 食べる (taberu, 'to eat') → 食べず (tabezu, 'without eating')
• 言う (iu, 'to say') → 言わず (iwazu, 'without saying')
• する (suru, 'to do') → せず (sezu, 'without doing')

Note: する → せず (not しず) is an irregular form to memorize. ず is common in written Japanese, formal speech, proverbs, and anime lyrics. 振り向かず進む (furimukazu susumu, 'advance without looking back').

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 構う (kamau, 'to care') → 構わない (kamawanai, negative) → 構わず (kamawazu, 'without caring')

grammar_points.name: 〜がままに (as one pleases)

explanation.en:
How it works: Place がままに (ga mama ni) after the dictionary form of a verb to express 'as one pleases' or 'according to'. It suggests following something naturally without resistance.

Example from this song: 信じるがままに (shinjiru ga mama ni) = 'as one believes / following what you believe' — from 信じる (shinjiru, 'to believe') + がままに (ga mama ni, 'as one pleases')

More examples:
• 思う (omou, 'to think') → 思うがままに (omou ga mama ni, 'as one thinks/wishes')
• 感じる (kanjiru, 'to feel') → 感じるがままに (kanjiru ga mama ni, 'as one feels')
• 流れる (nagareru, 'to flow') → 流れるがままに (nagareru ga mama ni, 'as it flows')

Note: This is a literary/formal expression. It conveys a philosophical acceptance — acting according to one's nature or instinct. 心のままに (kokoro no mama ni, 'as your heart wishes') is a related simpler pattern.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 信じる (shinjiru, 'to believe') + がままに (ga mama ni, 'as one pleases') → 信じるがままに (shinjiru ga mama ni, 'following what you believe')

grammar_points.name: 〜なんて (dismissive emphasis)

explanation.en:
How it works: Place なんて (nante) after a noun or phrase to add a dismissive or emphatic tone — 'things like' or 'something trivial like'. It shows the speaker's attitude toward what precedes it.

Example from this song: The lyrics use なんて to dismiss obstacles or conventional thinking, reinforcing the song's rebellious spirit.

More examples:
• 常識 (joushiki, 'common sense') → 常識なんて (joushiki nante, 'things like common sense — who needs it')
• 限界 (genkai, 'limit') → 限界なんてない (genkai nante nai, 'there's no such thing as limits')
• 失敗 (shippai, 'failure') → 失敗なんて怖くない (shippai nante kowakunai, 'I'm not afraid of something like failure')

Note: なんて can express dismissal, surprise, or defiance depending on context. In songs about freedom and determination (like GO!!!), it usually expresses defiance against limitations.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: [noun/phrase] + なんて (nante, 'things like — dismissive') = dismissive emphasis

grammar_points.name: 命令形 (imperative form)

explanation.en:
How it works: For godan verbs, change the final -u to -e. For ichidan verbs, replace る with ろ. This creates a direct, forceful command. An alternative masculine form uses ろ for godan verbs too in some dialects.

Example from this song: 見極めろ (mikiwamero) = 'Discern!' — from 見極める (mikiwameru, 'to discern') → 見極めろ (mikiwamero). Also 切り開け (kirihirake) = 'Carve open!' — from 切り開く (kirihiraku) → 切り開け

More examples:
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行け (ike, 'Go!')
• 起きる (okiru, 'to wake up') → 起きろ (okiro, 'Wake up!')
• する (suru, 'to do') → しろ (shiro, 'Do it!')

Note: The imperative is the quintessential anime battle-cry form. FLOW's GO!!! is full of these commands, creating an infectious energy. 走れ (hashire, 'Run!') and 行け (ike, 'Go!') are among the most iconic anime imperatives.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: 見極める (mikiwameru, 'to discern') → 見極めろ (mikiwamero, 'Discern!') / 切り開く (kirihiraku, 'to carve open') → 切り開け (kirihirake, 'Carve open!')

explanation.en:
How it works: Add だろう (darou) after a verb, adjective, or noun to express conjecture — 'probably' or 'I think'. With rising intonation, it seeks confirmation — 'right?'

Example from this song: The lyrics use だろう to both speculate and challenge — 'you know that, right?' or 'it's probably true, isn't it?'

More examples:
• 雨が降る (ame ga furu, 'it'll rain') → 雨が降るだろう (ame ga furu darou, 'it'll probably rain')
• 大丈夫 (daijoubu, 'OK') → 大丈夫だろう (daijoubu darou, 'it'll probably be fine')
• 知っている (shitteiru, 'know') → 知ってるだろう (shitteru darou, 'you know, right?')

Note: だろう is casual. でしょう (deshou) is the polite form. In anime, だろう with assertive tone = 'right?!' (challenging). With soft tone = 'probably' (speculation). でしょう with rising tone = 'isn't it?' (seeking agreement).

grammar_points.name: 〜てくぜ (gonna do it - masculine)

explanation.en:
How it works: Combine the て-form + いく (iku, 'to go') + ぜ (ze, masculine emphasis particle). This creates an energetic, masculine declaration — 'I'm gonna keep doing it!' The いく often contracts away.

Example from this song: The song uses this pattern to express determined forward momentum with a rough, energetic masculine tone.

More examples:
• 行く (iku, 'to go') → 行ってくぜ (ittekuze, 'I'm heading out!')
• やる (yaru, 'to do') → やってくぜ (yattekuze, 'I'm gonna do it!')
• 走る (hashiru, 'to run') → 走ってくぜ (hashittekuze, 'I'm gonna run!')

Note: ぜ (ze) is a rough masculine sentence-ending particle that adds energy and assertion. It's less aggressive than ぞ (zo). Common in shonen anime and J-rock. Think Naruto saying 行くってばよ (ikuttebayo) — similarly energetic but different particle.

grammar_points.conjugation_path: [te-form] + いく (iku, 'to go') + ぜ (ze, masculine emphasis) → てくぜ (tekuze, 'gonna do it!')
